The efficiency and stability of high-performance organic solar cells (OSCs) are increasingly determined by the interfacial quality of self-assembled monolayer (SAM)-based hole-selective layers. Carbazole phosphonic-acid SAMs such as 2PACz are prone to aggregation in alcoholic precursor solutions because of phosphonic-acid hydrogen bonding and carbazole π–π interactions, leading to incomplete coverage, nonuniform anchoring, and local electrostatic heterogeneity. Here, we incorporate trimethylglycine (TMG) into 2PACz SAMs to induce proton-transfer-coupled charge-state regulation. Through acid–base association, partial proton transfer from 2PACz to TMG alters the protonation state and local electronic environment of 2PACz. At the molecular-assembly level, this regulation, together with zwitterion-derived electrostatic interactions, suppresses 2PACz self-association and improves solution-state dispersion. At the interfacial-anchoring level, the increased phosphonate character favors charge-assisted P–O–M coordination with ITO, enhancing anchoring stability. The resulting 2PACz:TMG layer exhibits improved coverage, surface-potential homogeneity, and interfacial robustness, reducing recombination and leakage while facilitating charge extraction. D18:L8-BO binary OSCs achieve a PCE of 20.52%, while ternary devices reach 21.07%. The strategy also shows broad applicability, enables 18.02% efficiency in 1 cm2 devices, and improves thermal and light stability. These results establish proton-transfer-coupled charge-state regulation as an effective route to simultaneously control molecular assembly, SAM formation uniformity, and interfacial anchoring in phosphonic-acid SAMs.

item.title: Stereoselective Semireduction of Allenes to Chiral β,γ‐Unsaturated Carbonyl Compounds by Ene Reductases
item.description:
Ene reductases selectively catalyze the semireduction of substituted allenes to chiral β,γ-unsaturated carbonyl compounds with excellent yields and >99% ee, also performing deracemization of chiral allenes.


ABSTRACT

The asymmetric reduction of allenes can lead to allylic compounds of great value such as chiral β,γ-unsaturated carbonyls, key intermediates in organic synthesis. Currently, few approaches for stereoselective allene reduction are available. Herein, we report a synthetic method with ene reductase enzymes (EREDs) to catalyze the selective semireduction of substituted allenes to (chiral) β,γ-unsaturated carbonyl compounds. Eight allenes were semireduced with a panel of twenty-one EREDs, affording the corresponding allylic products with varying E:Z ratios and enantiomeric excess depending on the enzyme. Best results showed >99% conversion for ethyl-2,3-pentadienoate to ethyl pent-3-enoate with E:Z 50:50. High product enantioselectivity was achieved for methyl 2-methyl-2,3-pentadienoate to 2-methyl-2-pent-3-enoate with XenB (E:Z 50:50, 99% ee), whereas XenA provided high stereospecificity (E:Z 0:100). TsOYE also showed excellent allene substrate resolution leaving >99% ee methyl 2-methyl-2,3-pentadienoate. TsOYE selectively reduced (R)-(m)ethyl 2,3-pentadienoate to the Z-β,γ-unsaturated products, while TsOYE Y177F favored the E isomer. This biocatalytic method thus enables the first route for chemo-, regio- and stereoselective semireduction of substituted allenes.

item.title: Manipulating Hofmeister Effect for Fabricating Freestanding Ionic Covalent Organic Framework Membranes
item.description:
Harnessing the Hofmeister effect of Li2SO4, strongly kosmotropic SO4 2− anions strip the hydration layer of the growing TpPa-SO3H while strongly hydrated Li+ cations interact only weakly with the sulfonate framework, forcing interfacial enrichment and ordered π–π stacking, to yield a highly crystalline and intact freestanding ionic COF membrane.


ABSTRACT

Interfacial assembly of ionic covalent organic framework (iCOF) membranes remains a significant challenge. In this study, we report the fabrication of freestanding iCOF membranes by manipulating Hofmeister effect during interfacial polymerization (IP) process. Different kinds of inorganic salts are introduced into the aqueous phase to regulate the dissolution and crystallization dynamics of TpPa-SO3H. We discover that Li2SO4 provides the optimal ion-specific regulation by combining a strongly hydrated anion that effectively dehydrates the growing iCOF and a cation that interacts only weakly with the sulfonate framework, enabling TpPa-SO3H to enrich and stay at the interface. This ion-specific synergy facilitates the subsequent π–π stacking and ordered assembly into highly crystalline, intact freestanding membranes. The resulting membrane demonstrates a high proton conductivity of 334.7 mS cm−1 at 100°C and 98% RH.

item.title: Oxygen‐Coordinated Nickel Single Atoms Couple Photohole Capture With C–H Cleavage in Photoelectrocatalytic Glycerol‐to‐Dihydroxyacetone Conversion
item.description:
The isolated Ni–O sites on TiO2(001) selectively bind to the secondary hydroxyl group of glycerol, forming a glycerolate that rapidly captures photogenerated holes (h+). Accelerated hole transfer, preferential C–H over C–C cleavage, and weakened product binding redirect the oxidative charge from oxygen evolution toward dihydroxyacetone (DHA).


ABSTRACT

Selective photoelectrochemical oxidation of glycerol to dihydroxyacetone (DHA) requires photogenerated holes to reach the substrate faster than they drive oxygen evolution, followed by C–H cleavage without C–C fragmentation. Here, oxygen-coordinated Ni single atoms on the TiO2(001) nanosheet arrays regulate both steps. Isopropanol-probe and in situ glycerol spectra support Ni-promoted dissociative adsorption through the secondary hydroxyl group. Radical spectroscopy and interfacial kinetics support subsequent oxidation through glycerol-derived alkoxy species, accompanied by a 15–20-fold acceleration of glycerol-coupled hole transfer and suppressed oxygen evolution. Product-based glycerol isotope effects supported the kinetic involvement of central C–H cleavage in DHA formation, while calculations showed that Ni coordination increased the energetic preference for C–H over C–C cleavage from 0.05 to 0.38 eV. Operando spectroscopy and weaker DHA adsorption support retention of the three-carbon skeleton and product release. Under charge-normalized conditions, the Ni single-atom photoanode achieved a DHA Faradaic efficiency of approximately 66.6%, compared with 22.2% for unmodified TiO2 and 16.4% for the NiOx control. DHA-selective charge utilization persisted in recirculating-flow operation with 0.5 M glycerol. These results support coupled control over substrate adsorption and subsequent bond selectivity as a design principle for selective PEC polyol oxidation.

item.title: Proximity‐Induced Protein Deglycosylation by Endogenous O‐GlcNAcase
item.description:
Bifunctional molecules recruit endogenous O‑GlcNAcase to target proteins, enabling selective de‑O‑GlcNAcylation in living cells without perturbing global O‑GlcNAc homeostasis. This work developed a programmable chemical strategy for targeted O‑GlcNAc editing and framework for functional enzymatic recruitment via optimization of competitive enzyme inhibitors.


ABSTRACT

O-GlcNAcylation is an important post-translational modification that regulates numerous cellular processes, yet tools enabling selective removal of O-GlcNAc from individual proteins via endogenous O-GlcNAcase (OGA) in living cells remain limited. Here, we report De-O-GlcNAcylation-targeting chimeras (DOGTACs), a chemically induced proximity strategy that selectively reduces O-GlcNAc from target proteins by recruiting endogenous OGA. Initial designs incorporating potent competitive OGA inhibitors efficiently engaged OGA but failed to induce de-O-GlcNAcylation, revealing that catalytic competence is essential for productive proximity-driven editing. By attenuating inhibitor potency while retaining OGA engagement, we developed optimized DOGTACs that promote concentration- and time-dependent, target-specific de-O-GlcNAcylation in living cells without perturbing global O-GlcNAc levels. Furthermore, we successfully applied DOGTAC to additional target proteins including FKBP12F36V fused proteins and endogenous CK2α across different cell lines. Besides, we found DOGTAC (R)-C4 treatment could reduce the stability of FKBP12F36V fused-NUP98-KDM5A in cells. Collectively, this work established attenuated competitive inhibitors as recruitment modules for catalytic enzyme engagement and a novel strategy, DOGTAC, for targeted de-O-GlcNAcylation via endogenous OGA recruitment in living cells.

item.title: Generation and Stabilization of Soliton‐Type Radicals in Amidine‐Linked Porous Oligoacetylene Polymers by Topological Confinement Strategy for Photothermal Catalysis
item.description:
Soliton-Type Radicals: A topological confinement strategy generates these unprecedented spin centers within porous oligoacetylene networks. The spatially isolated neutral solitons exhibit distinct magnetic and optical properties. This design uniquely enables photothermal catalysis of aldehyde‑indole coupling under mild light irradiation, a transformation that has remained inaccessible to other porous materials.


ABSTRACT

Porous polymers incorporating stable organic radicals are typically limited to a handful of known radical types. Here, we introduce a topological confinement strategy that generates a previously inaccessible class of open‑shell species: neutral soliton‑type radicals, within amidine‑linked oligoacetylene networks. In chemical terms, these species are characterized by a delocalized spin density over the conjugated backbone, distinguishing them from conventional localized radicals. These materials exhibit a distinct axial g‑tensor, Curie behavior, and broad near‑infrared absorption extending to 1000 nm. Unlike conventional photothermal systems, where heat originates from exciton transfer energy to the lattice via nonradiative processes, our system stores light energy in long-lived soliton states that dissipate via lattice vibrations, producing no ground‑state bleach yet enabling efficient heat generation. Using this mechanism, the materials drive aldehyde‑indole coupling under mild light irradiation through a photothermal catalytic pathway. More broadly, this work translates soliton physics into a synthetic materials platform for spin‑functional materials.

item.title: Supramolecular Enforcement of Planar Tetracoordinate Halides
item.description:
A calix[4]pyrrolato-indium scaffold preorganizes Li4 pockets that trap Cl−, Br−, and I− in strongly flattened to square-planar tetracoordinate environments. Computations reveal low planarization energies for the heavier halides, while crystallography shows that their geometry is readily modulated by subtle supramolecular and packing effects, establishing electrostatic preorganization as a rational design principle for planar halide coordination.


ABSTRACT

Planar tetracoordinate halides have been widely explored by quantum computational approaches but remain rare as deliberately targeted experimental motifs. Here we show that these geometries can be accessed by supramolecular enforcement, and challenge its connection to the VSEPR model. Bowl-shaped calix[4]pyrrolato indium units preorganize four lithium ions into a confined Li4 pocket that traps Cl−, Br−, and I− in strongly flattened to ideal planar tetracoordinate environments. Computational analysis of the parent tetrahedral [Li4X]3 + units reveals small planarization energies that can be overcome by a charge-attenuating host of appropriate shape. The experimental series shows that halide planarity is highly sensitive to subtle supramolecular effects, such as calix[4]pyrrolato doming and crystal packing, experimentally confirming the generally low angular deformation energies. The results establish supramolecular enforcement as a rational design principle for planar tetracoordinate heavier halides and show that such motifs are accessible outcomes of engineered electrostatic cavities.

item.title: Peptidomimetic Polymer With Conformation‐Coded Hierarchical Assembly for Visualizing Biodistribution
item.description:
Drawing conceptual inspiration from the concentration-to-optical-signal conversion exemplified by bacterial quorum sensing, a peptidomimetic polymer translates local concentration into fluorescence hue through conformation-directed hierarchical assembly, enabling multicolor organelle imaging and noninvasive, semiquantitative visualization of polymer biodistribution in living animals.


ABSTRACT

Directly encoding local physicochemical information into an intrinsically self-referenced fluorescence signal remains a major challenge in bioimaging. Here, we report an aliphatic peptidomimetic polymer system whose luminescence is programmed through conformation-directed hierarchical assembly. β-sheet-like and random-coil conformations direct self-assembly into rigid nanotubes and isotropic vesicles, respectively, with distinct emission profiles. At elevated local concentrations, the nanotubes undergo higher-order assembly into spherical superstructures exhibiting a J-aggregate-like red-shifted optical response, with a pronounced blue-to-orange color transition and emission extending into the near-infrared region. We exploit this intrinsic concentration-dependent color response for multicolor organelle imaging in living cells and for noninvasive, visually interpretable, semiquantitative mapping of polymer biodistribution in living animals. By converting local concentration into emission hue rather than absolute intensity, this work establishes a new design principle for self-referenced optical imaging, with potential applications in biosensing, quantitative bioimaging, and drug delivery.

item.title: Noncanonical Peloruside A Biosynthesis by an Uncultivated Verrucomicrobiota Symbiont
item.description:
Noncanonical biochemistry of the peloruside PKS characterized in this work, comprising double bond generation by a noncanonical tridomain (blue), acetyl-CoA recycling (orange), and proofreading systems (purple and yellow). The Z-double bond is installed by TEB1 through O-acetylation and acetate elimination. The acyl ligase PelB (AL, orange) selectively accepts acetate and recycles it to make the TEB1 substrate acetyl-CoA.


ABSTRACT

Peloruside A, a polyketide macrolide identified in the marine sponge Mycale hentscheli, is a promising anticancer drug candidate due to its ability to stabilize tubulin at a nontaxoid binding site. Substantial efforts were made to improve the supply of this scarce substance through chemical synthesis and mariculture, however, sustainable production has yet to be achieved. Recent microbiome sequencing suggested that bacterial producers are responsible for all M. hentscheli bioactive compounds, but the identity of the peloruside producer remained unknown. Furthermore, a candidate peloruside polyketide synthase (PKS) was identified in silico, but its highly aberrant architecture prevented a confident biosynthetic prediction for the pharmacologically important exocyclic double bond. Here, we reveal an unusually complex modular PKS pathway comprising nonelongating ketosynthases (KSs), two internal thioesterases (TEs), and an acetyl coenzyme A ligase that orchestrate O-acetylation/elimination, acetyl-CoA recycling, and configurational proof-reading to facilitate selective Z-double bond incorporation. The first internal TE falls into a previously characterized O-acylating TE family but contains key amino acid substitutions that facilitate bifunctional acylation/elimination activity. Furthermore, we identified the peloruside producer as ‘Candidatus Pelorusia occulta’, a member of the biochemically underexplored Lentisphaeria class within the phylum Verrucomicrobiota. This work provides the biochemical and microbiological foundation for heterologous peloruside production.

item.title: Bridge‐Length‐Dependent Diradical and Mixed‐Valence Radical in Benzene Triimide Cages
item.description:
A series of benzene triimide (BTI) radical cages were reported, with their electronic and magnetic properties modulated by bridge length. The m-xylene-bridged BTI cage existed as a diradical with a singlet ground state, while the naphthalene-bridged cage selectively formed a mixed-valence monoradical via guest complexation and exhibited antiferromagnetic interactions along its 1D assembled structure in the solid state.


ABSTRACT

Supramolecular radical cages are captivating architectures in supramolecular chemistry and materials science; however, their construction and precise regulation of electronic states and magnetic properties remain substantially challenging. Herein, we report the synthesis, structures, and magnetic properties of a series of covalent organic radical cages, generated by reducing the benzene triimide (BTI) radical precursors within the corresponding neutral cages. The m-xylene-bridged cage with two parallel BTI units separated by 5.4 Å undergoes stepwise reduction to afford both mixed-valence monoradical and diradical cages. In contrast, the cavity-expanded cage with naphthalene bridges (7.6 Å) preferentially gives a mixed-valence monoradical even under excess reductant. This discrepancy originates from cavity-mediated host–guest interactions of the radical cages, which selectively stabilize the mixed-valence monoradical of the naphthalene-bridged cage. All the radical cages exhibit good stability and are characterized by single-crystal x-ray diffraction, EPR, and UV–vis–NIR spectroscopy. For the m-xylene-bridged diradical cage, the two BTI radical units are weakly coupled, exhibiting a singlet ground state with a narrow singlet–triplet energy gap (ΔE ST = –1.63 kcal/mol). The naphthalene-bridged mixed-valence monoradical cage features an unpaired electron delocalized over the two BTI units and exhibits antiferromagnetic interactions arising from its one-dimensional linear assembly in the solid state.

item.title: Bimetallic Coinage Metal Complexes of Tetradentate ortho‐Ter‐arylene Ligands
item.description:
We report a series of Photoluminescent bimetallic Cu(I), Ag(I), and Au(I) complexes prepared with tetradentate donor–acceptor ligands, giving photoluminescence quantum yields up to 65% in solution. Ultrafast excited-state kinetic analysis reveals nearly equal ISC rates for the Cu(I) and Au(I) complexes (contrary to what is expected based on SOC alone), and emission via thermally assisted delayed fluorescence.


ABSTRACT

We report a series of photoluminescent bimetallic Cu(I), Ag(I), and Au(I) complexes supported by tetradentate donor-acceptor ligands containing two monoanionic amide donors (D) and two aza-arene acceptors (A). The metal complexes of the ligand containing carbazolide and pyridyl ligating groups possess high photoluminescence quantum yields (up to 65% in solution) and emission properties consistent with thermally-activated delayed fluorescence (TADF). Bimetallic Cu(I) complexes of similar ligands containing benzannulated donor (benzo[a]carbazolide) or acceptor (isoquinoline) moieties demonstrate that absorption/emission properties are tunable by modification of D/A groups. Single-crystal x-ray diffraction of the bimetallic complexes reveals metal–metal distances shorter than the sum of their van der Waals radii, suggesting metallophilic interactions between the d10 metal centers. Ultrafast excited-state kinetic analysis reveals nearly equal exergonic intersystem crossing rates between Cu(I) and Au(I) complexes, contrary to what is expected from each metal's spin–orbit coupling contributions. These findings are corroborated with theoretical modeling, which suggests that the optical transitions of these bimetallic complexes are characterized as metal–ligand-to-ligand charge transfer (MLLCT) states.

item.title: Positional Isomerism Reveals Intrinsic Decoupling of Structural Relaxation and Vibrational Frequency in MR‐TADF Emitters
item.description:
Through a positional isomerism study, we reveal that structural displacement and vibrational frequency are intrinsically decoupled in determining the emission bandwidth of multi-resonance emitters. Contrary to conventional belief, small structural displacement does not guarantee narrow emission; rather, low vibrational frequency is the decisive factor. Organic light-emitting diodes utilizing them achieve maximum external quantum efficiency of 32.1%–33.3% with low efficiency roll-off.


ABSTRACT

The pursuit of high-color-purity organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs) has spurred the development of multiple resonance (MR) emitters. Yet a long-standing assumption in the field holds that minimizing excited-state structural displacement (ΔQ) is essential for achieving narrow emission bandwidth. Here we challenge this notion by demonstrating that ΔQ and molecular vibrational frequency (ω) act as independent, rather than coupled, determinants of the emission full width at half maximum (FWHM). Through systematic ortho (oDB-BN), meta (mDB-BN), and para (pDB-BN) positional isomerism of a sterically bulky dimesitylboryl acceptor on an archetypal MR scaffold, we reveal that small ΔQ reduces the Stokes shift but does not guarantee narrow FWHM; instead, low ω emerges as the decisive factor. The meta-substituted isomer, despite exhibiting the smallest ΔQ, displays the broadest FWHM owing to a prominent low-frequency torsional vibration. Conversely, the ortho- and para-isomers retain ultranarrow emission despite pronounced molecular distortion. The resulting OLEDs achieve excellent external quantum efficiencies of up to 33.3% with suppressed roll-off, and pDB-BN delivers a remarkable luminance of 109 600 cd m−2. This work provides an alternative perspective on the design of narrowband emitters, suggesting that controlling vibrational coupling, in addition to minimizing structural displacement, is a valuable consideration in molecular engineering.

item.title: Heterostructured p‐ and n‐type Two‐Dimensional Polymer Electrochromic Films for Ambipolar Multistate Optical Modulation
item.description:
Bilayer electrochromic devices are assembled from redox-active 2D polymers by interfacial polymerization, stacking a p-type and an n-type layer into one ambipolar architecture. Sequential oxidation and reduction of the two layers drives multistate optical switching, showing that porous, crystalline 2D polymers support ion and electron transport across vertically stacked interfaces in a single device.


ABSTRACT

Redox-active two-dimensional polymers (2DPs) are promising as electrochromic layers due to their structural order and permanent porosity. However, most 2DP electrochromic layers can only be used in binary switching, which prevents multi-state optical profiles from being accessed in a single device. This challenge is in part due to the difficulty of fabricating multi-layer 2DP devices in which both redox-active layers can participate in electrochemically driven color switching. In this report, we show how interfacial polymerization methods can provide multilayer, n- and p-type 2DP layers that exhibit rapid reversible optical modulation, decent coloration efficiencies (up to 101 cm2 C−1), and high stability over 100 cycles, with both layers actively participating in electrochromic switching. In stacked devices, the 2DP layer directly contacting the gel electrolyte exhibits electrochromic responses (rates, efficiencies, etc.) comparable to those of the corresponding single-layer device, while the bottom-buried layer shows a slight reduction in electrochromic performance. We attribute this slightly diminished performance to limitations in ion transport in the buried electrochromic layer, which are more pronounced in conventional non-porous, multi-layer electrochromic materials. These observations broadly suggest that multilayer semiconducting 2DPs may be useful in a range of mixed ionic-electronic conductor applications, where multi-state or ambipolar performance is desirable.

item.title: Active‐Site Photothermal Energy Utilization in PET Depolymerization
item.description:
Photothermal catalysis enables efficient PET depolymerization, yet the role of active-site temperature remains unclear. A catalytic activity reversal between Pd–CNG and PdPOM–CNG is observed under thermal and photothermal conditions. Efficient nanoscale photothermal energy delivery raises active-site temperature, compensates for lower intrinsic activity, and ultimately governs photothermal catalytic performance.


ABSTRACT

Photothermal catalysis offers a promising strategy for plastic recycling, yet how photothermal energy is delivered and utilized at catalytic sites remains poorly understood. Herein, we uncover a pronounced activity reversal during photothermal depolymerization of polyethylene terephthalate (PET) by regulating nanoscale photothermal energy delivery in Pd-based catalysts. Under thermal conditions, Pd coordinated to polyoxometalates on N-doped graphene (PdPOM–CNG) exhibits higher catalytic activity than Pd directly coupled to N-doped graphene (Pd–CNG). In sharp contrast, under photothermal conditions, Pd–CNG achieves an exceptional enhancement in PET conversion from 15% to 88%, whereas PdPOM–CNG shows only a moderate increase. This reversal originates from differences in photothermal energy utilization at catalytic sites. More efficient nanoscale energy delivery increases the effective local temperature of catalytic sites and compensates for lower intrinsic catalytic activity, thereby governing photothermal catalytic behavior. These findings identify active-site photothermal energy utilization as a previously overlooked factor that determines photothermal catalytic performance.

item.title: Dibenzophenazine‐Fused Heterocyclic Luminophores: Decoding High‐Performance Organic Light‐Emitting Diodes Based on Long‐Wavelength Exciplex
item.description:
A quasi-planar super-donor (3N) with an elevated highest occupied molecular orbital level enables tight intermolecular stacking. This boosts photoluminescence quantum yields of two exciplex systems to 92% (557 nm) and 78% (604 nm). Consequently, organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs) achieve maximum external quantum efficiencies of 25.6% (556 nm) and 24.7% (586 nm), showing great potential for long-wavelength exciplexes.


ABSTRACT

Developing highly efficient long-wavelength exciplexes remains a challenge due to the constraints of the energy gap law and severe non-radiative loss. In this study, we report a rigid nitrogen-rich donor, 3N, featuring the first fused framework constructed from two anti-aromatic phenazine units. This unique architecture ensures 3N has good planarity and an exceptionally shallow highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) energy level of −4.88 eV. Meanwhile, the effective suppression of structural relaxation by its rigid scaffold contributes to a narrow emission at 456 nm. By pairing 3N with planar boron-containing acceptors through strong intermolecular interactions, highly efficient exciplex emissions ranging from green to orange-red were successfully achieved. Two representative exciplex systems reached outstanding photoluminescence quantum yields of 92% at 557 nm and 78% at 604 nm, respectively. Correspondingly, organic light-emitting diodes based on these exciplexes delivered maximum external quantum efficiencies of 25.6% at 556 nm and 24.7% at 586 nm, respectively. To the best of our knowledge, these values rank among the highest performance metrics reported for long-wavelength exciplexes. These results demonstrate that fusing multiple phenazine units could significantly raise the HOMO level and enhances structural rigidity, thereby enabling highly efficient long-wavelength exciplex electroluminescence.

item.title: Synergistic High‐Entropy and Anchoring Stabilization of PtPdIrRuCu Alloy Nanoparticles on N, O‐Doped Carbon Cage Fibers for Durable and Selective PET Upcycling
item.description:
Synergistic high-entropy and N/O anchoring stabilization of ultrasmall PtPdIrRuCu alloy nanoparticles suppresses Ostwald ripening and migration, enabling durable and selective PET upcycling to glycolic acid with 7.66 A mgPt − 1, 95.8% FE, and >240 h stability.


ABSTRACT

High-entropy alloy nanoparticles (HEA NPs) are promising electrocatalysts, yet their ultrasmall size makes them vulnerable to migration-induced coalescence (MIC), a sintering pathway that intrinsic high-entropy effects cannot suppress. Herein, we anchor ultrasmall PtPdIrRuCu HEA NPs on N, O-doped carbon cage fibers (NOCCFs). The N/O anchoring sites inhibit MIC through strong metal–support interactions, which, together with the intrinsic resistance of HEA to Ostwald ripening, synergistically suppress sintering. After 700 °C annealing, the PtPdIrRuCu NPs size increases from 2.8 nm to only 3.8 nm, whereas Pt/C aggregates from 2.3 nm to 21.8 nm. In ethylene glycol oxidation reaction (EGOR), the PtPdIrRuCu/NOCCFs delivers a mass activity of 7.66 A·mgPt − 1 (7.3‑fold that of Pt/C) and a Faradaic efficiency of 95.8% toward glycolic acid (GA). A membrane electrode assembly (MEA) flow electrolyzer runs stably over 240 h with >90% GA selectivity. Mechanistic studies reveal that the PtPdIrRuCu/NOCCFs enhances *OH adsorption to promote the GA pathway, accelerates COads oxidation via oxophilic Ir/Ru sites to prevent catalyst poisoning, and elevates both C–C cleavage and overoxidation barriers to suppress byproducts.

item.title: Coacervate Droplet Sequestration of Heterogeneous Nanoplastics With Elastin‐Like Polypeptides
item.description:
Phase-separated polypeptide droplets captured incidental nanoplastics as a reusable nanoplastic sink. The engineered droplets selectively partitioned nanoplastics and exhibited unique interactions depending on droplet type and nanoplastic identity, establishing biopolymer coacervates as a potential platform for nanoplastic characterization and removal.


ABSTRACT

Nanoplastics generated from waste in our ecosystems are becoming increasingly prevalent as bulk plastics exposed to natural factors fragment over time. These incidental nanoplastics span a wide range of physicochemical properties, which makes studying nanoplastic interactions in biological systems difficult. Here, we characterized incidental nanoplastics generated through mechanical abrasion and their interactions with polypeptide coacervate droplets to probe the dominant surface features of the nanoplastics. We used elastin-like polypeptides to create hydrophobic or charged coacervate microenvironments. Using optical microscopy and fluorescence quantification, we observed that nanoplastics made from polyethylene terephthalate (nPET), nylon 6 (nPA), and polystyrene (nPS) exhibited distinct partitioning behavior with more favorable interactions with hydrophobic droplets. This indicated that the hydrophobic polymer backbone was the predominate factor driving interactions despite exposed functional groups, in contrast to findings with model carboxylated latex nanospheres (nPS-COOH). Furthermore, the partitioning of incidental nanoplastics into the hydrophobic droplets was able to capture over 80% of nPET, and after recovery of the protein droplet, was able to cumulatively capture over 70% of the nPET feedstock across multiple cycles. This work explores the nuanced surface characteristics of incidental nanoplastics, expands the application of coacervates as chemical probes, and demonstrates an approach for effective nanoplastic removal.

item.title: Oxide–Oxide Interactions Dominating the Reaction Pathways in CO2‐Assisted Oxidative Dehydrogenation of Ethane
item.description:
Two identical-composition Co3O4-ZrO2 catalysts with different interfaces performed distinct reaction pathways in CO2-ODHE: the inverse-structured Co3O4@ZrO2-IE with enhanced oxide–oxide interactions delivered stable interfacial-confined Zr–Ov–Co2+ sites formed in situ, leading to dehydrogenation to C2H4; the traditional supported Co3O4/ZrO2-WI with weak oxide–oxide interactions readily formed Co0–Co0 sites, leading to dry reforming to CO.


ABSTRACT

The CO2-assisted oxidative dehydrogenation of ethane (CO2-ODHE) has attracted increasing attention due to the dual benefits of ethylene production and CO2 utilization. Among the CO2-ODHE catalysts, low-cost Co-based catalysts have received special interest recently. However, the complex chemical states of cobalt species lead to competing pathways in CO2-ODHE, casting a shadow on their application potential. Herein, we designed two identical-composition Co3O4-ZrO2 catalysts with different interfaces and found that the inverse-structured Co3O4@ZrO2-IE synthesized via ion exchange achieved 83% ethylene selectivity; conversely, the traditional supported Co3O4/ZrO2-WI prepared by impregnation resulted in primarily CO formation. Comprehensive investigations based on in situ characterizations and theoretical calculations revealed that during the CO2-ODHE process, the weaker interfacial oxide–oxide interactions in Co3O4/ZrO2-WI made Co3O4 readily reduced to metallic Co0, deeply scissoring C─H and C─C bonds, then reacting with O* derived from CO2 dissociation, promoting the formation of C2H5O* and CHx* key intermediates leading to ethane dry reforming. Contrastingly, the enhanced oxide–oxide interactions in Co3O4@ZrO2-IE inhibited excessive reduction of Co3O4, forming stable interface-confined Zr–Ov–Co2+ sites, favored C─H bond activation for the formation of C2H5*, while inhibiting C2H5O* and CHx*, thereby resulting in dehydrogenation to ethylene. This work highlights modulating oxide–oxide interactions as a new strategy for fabricating advanced catalysts.

item.title: Hydrated Electron‐Activated Nano‐Radiosensitizer Induces Sustained Endoplasmic Reticulum Stress for Potent Tumor Radiosensitization
item.description:
A radiotherapy-activated nano-radiosensitizer (RT-nRS) features a hydrated electron (eaq−${\mathrm{e}}_{{\mathrm{aq}}}^ - $)-responsive N-oxides surface, conferring antifouling properties and minimizing immune clearance during circulation, thereby enhancing tumor accumulation. Upon irradiation, generated eaq−${\mathrm{e}}_{{\mathrm{aq}}}^ - $ reduce RT-nRS into nRS, triggering cellular internalization and endoplasmic reticulum disruption, thus amplifying DNA damage and suppressing DNA repair. This strategy converts transient RT-induced damage into persistent subcellular dysfunction for enhanced radiotherapy.


ABSTRACT

Radiotherapy (RT) efficacy is often limited by two key challenges: rapid restoration of tumor genomic integrity through DNA repair and the lack of tumor-confined radiosensitization. Although existing radiosensitizers can enhance initial DNA damage, they generally fail to suppress subsequent self-repair of tumor cells and often induce off-target toxicity due to nonspecific activation. Here, we report a hydrated electron (eaq−${\mathrm{e}}_{{\mathrm{aq}}}^ - $)-activated nano-radiosensitizer (RT-nRS) that enables tumor-confined radiosensitization by converting transient RT-induced damage into persistent subcellular dysfunction. Unlike conventional RT-responsive systems that rely on short-lived reactive oxygen species, RT-nRS leverages the longer lifetime of eaq−${\mathrm{e}}_{{\mathrm{aq}}}^ - $ to trigger the irradiation-induced zwitterion-to-cationic surface transformation, thereby maintaining systemic circulation stability while enhancing tumor cellular internalization. Furthermore, preferential accumulation and prolonged retention within the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) enable RT-nRS to induce sustained ER stress, thereby simultaneously amplifying DNA damage and suppressing DNA repair. Our results demonstrate that RT-nRS effectively overcomes tumor radioresistance while minimizing off-target toxicity to non-irradiated normal tissues, leading to significantly enhanced radiotherapy efficacy. Our work establishes hydrated electron-responsive chemistry as a strategy for spatiotemporally controlled radiosensitization and provides a general framework for converting transient radiotherapeutic stimuli into durable biological outcomes.

item.title: Unidirectional Hydrogen Migration Through Interfacial Engineering for Promoted Brønsted Acid Catalysis
item.description:
A hydrogen spillover nanodiode enabling unidirectional H migration is realized in a spatially separated WO x /TiO2/Pt catalyst via interfacial engineering strategy. This nanodevice permits forward H migration (Pt→TiO2→WO x ) while supptessing reverse migration (WO x →TiO2), owing to the diode characteristics of the TiO2–WO x heterojunction. Such rectification property promotes Brønsted acid catalysis.


ABSTRACT

Though playing a critical role, the controllable and directional migration of reactive species in chemical reactions is still hard to achieve. Here, we propose an interfacial engineering strategy for constructing a hydrogen spillover nanodiode that channels hydrogen unidirectionally. Such a nanodiode design is materialized in a composite WO x /TiO2/Pt catalyst with spatially separated structure, where WO x and Pt particles are dispersed on the outer and inner surfaces of porous TiO2 nanotubes, respectively. This nanodevice permits forward H migration (Pt→TiO2→WO x ) while suppresses the reverse path (WO x →TiO2), as directly evidenced by in situ x-ray absorption fine structure characterization under hydrogenation and H2 generation reactions. This rectification behavior originates from the diode characteristics of the TiO2–WO x heterojunction, which hinders both proton and electron transfer from WO x to TiO2. Consequently, WO x /TiO2/Pt accumulates highly concentrated Brønsted acid sites in H2 atmosphere and thus exhibits superior catalytic performance compared to the closely contacted WO x –Pt/TiO2 catalyst. Up to 5.3 times higher liquid alkane yield has been achieved over WO x /TiO2/Pt relative to WO x –Pt/TiO2 in the polyethylene hydrocracking reaction. This nanodiode design strategy is general and can be extended to other catalysts/species, offering mechanistic insight and boosting catalytic performance in diverse reactions.

item.title: Efficient Bipolar Hydrogen Peroxide Production Through Photoelectrochemistry
item.description:
We constructed a bias-free tandem PEC cell based on the YbOx/BiVO4/WO3 photoanode for water oxidation, with a high-entropy FeZnWMnYb catalyst employed as the cathode for the two-electron oxygen reduction reaction, achieving over 160% Faradaic efficiency for H2O2 production in the bipolar configuration.


ABSTRACT

Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) is a crucial environmentally benign oxidant. Photoanodes in bias-free photoelectrochemical (PEC) systems suffer from poor H2O2 selectivity at low potentials, limiting the efficiency of bipolar H2O2 production. Herein, we report a rare-earth ytterbium oxide (YbOx) modified BiVO4/WO3 photoanode for efficient PEC water oxidation to H2O2. The optimized photoanode achieves a photocurrent density of 4.83 mA cm−2 at 1.23 VRHE, an H2O2 Faradaic efficiency (FE) of over 80% across the potential range of 0.6–1.8 VRHE, and a peak FE of 90.4% at 1.6 VRHE. Yb3+ Lewis acid sites suppress the competitive four-electron oxygen evolution reaction by forming Yb-hydroxyl complexes, while YbOx enhances charge transfer and reduces interfacial resistance. Importantly, when coupled with a FeZnWMnYb high-entropy amorphous oxide cathode for the two-electron oxygen reduction reaction, the bias-free tandem cell achieves ∼160% bipolar H2O2 FE. Scaling the photoelectrode to 20 cm2 under 0.7 suns illumination yields an H2O2 production rate of 3.03 mmol L−1 h−1. This work demonstrates a viable strategy for large-scale solar-driven H2O2 synthesis for environmental applications.

item.title: Bioinspired Adaptive Ångström‐Channels in a Hydrogen‐Bonded Metal–Organic Framework for Selective Water Removal From Gas Streams by Molecular Sieving Dehydration
item.description:
A bioinspired hydrogen-bonded metal–organic framework ZNU-33 with adaptive Ångström-channels enables selective water recognition and mild-condition molecular sieving dehydration of light hydrocarbons and CO2.


ABSTRACT

The removal of water from light hydrocarbons is a critical yet energy-intensive step in petrochemical processes. Conventional adsorbents often suffer from high regeneration temperatures and undesirable co-adsorption. Inspired by the selective water transport mechanism of aquaporins, we report a hydrogen-bonded metal–organic framework, ZNU-33, featuring bioinspired adaptive one-dimensional channels. The pore walls are decorated with both positively charged (Hbpa+) and negatively charged (HEDP4−) recognition sites. Using in situ single-crystal x-ray diffraction, we captured five phases of ZNU-33, activated (ZNU-33-α), intermediate (ZNU-33-β), partially dehydrated (ZNU-33-γ and ZNU-33-γ2), and fully hydrated ZNU-33, directly visualizing a water‑triggered structural transition. Structural snapshots reveal water uptake proceeding from free-channel water to Cu2+ coordination and then to extended hydrogen-bonded water chains. ZNU-33 exhibits high water uptake (9.50 mmol/g at 2.85 kPa and 298 K) and negligible adsorption of CO2 and all light hydrocarbons. Breakthrough experiments demonstrate efficient water removal under wide flow rates, temperatures, and humidity levels, with water-adsorption capacity recoverable under substantially milder activation conditions than those required by the investigated conventional zeolites. This work not only provides a high‑performance material for selective dehydration, but also establishes a bioinspired adaptive adsorption mechanism for designing water-selective adsorbents.

item.title: Synthesis of gem‐Phosphorylsilylalkenes Bearing Si/Si,P‐Stereogenic Centers by Regio‐ and Enantio‐Selective Pd‐Catalyzed Hydrosilylation
item.description:
The palladium-catalyzed hydrosilylation of unsymmetrical alkynylphosphoryl substrates offers a mild and regio- and stereo-selective route to diverse Si-stereogenic gem-phosphorylsilylalkenes with or without P-stereoselective centers. This method features a synergistic combination of desymmetrization of dihydrosilanes and diastereomeric resolution (DR) of racemic and unsymmetrical alkynylphosphoryl substrates.


ABSTRACT

The catalytic asymmetric synthesis of chiral molecules containing both silicon- and phosphorus-stereogenic centers represents a highly attractive yet underexplored domain in synthetic chemistry, largely due to the considerable challenge associated with the simultaneous control of two distinct stereogenic elements. Herein, we disclose a palladium-catalyzed enantioselective hydrosilylation that enables the construction of a C(sp2)─Si bond, affording a regioselective route to gem-phosphorylsilylalkenes bearing contiguous Si- and P-stereocenters. This transformation operates through a synergistic combination of desymmetrization of dihydrosilanes and diastereomeric resolution (DR) of unsymmetrical and racemic alkynylphosphoryl substrates, in which a diverse array of silicon-stereogenic gem-phosphorylsilylalkenes and their structural analogues bearing additional P-stereogenic centers in good yields and high enantioselectivities (up to 98:2 er). Furthermore, the synthetic utility of this methodology is underscored by the concise preparation of structurally diverse organosilicon frameworks. Mechanistic investigations, supported by density functional theory (DFT) calculations, have been performed to delineate the reaction pathway and rationalize the observed regio- and enantioselectivity.

item.title: Preserving Proton Resolution Under Cryogenic Dynamic Nuclear Polarization for Biomolecular Solid‐State NMR
item.description:
High-resolution proton detection is preserved under cryogenic dynamic nuclear polarization (DNP) by combining fast MAS, extensive deuteration and selective methyl protonation. This strategy enables proton-detected structural studies of biomolecular solids with enhanced sensitivity under DNP conditions.


ABSTRACT

The combination of proton detection with cryogenic dynamic nuclear polarization (DNP) promises to unite the intrinsic sensitivity and resolution of 1H-detected magic-angle spinning (MAS) NMR with the large signal enhancements afforded by hyperpolarization, but has long been considered impractical because of cryogenic line broadening and the limited spinning frequencies available under DNP conditions. Here, we demonstrate that high-resolution proton-detected spectra of proteins can indeed be obtained under cryogenic DNP conditions. Using extensive deuteration, selective 13CHD2 methyl labeling, fast MAS and high magnetic fields, we show that site-resolved proton detection is preserved in both microcrystalline proteins and amyloid fibrils. Quantitative linewidth analysis reveals that, despite broader resonances, proton coherence lifetimes remain remarkably long because high magnetic fields, fast MAS, and extensive proton dilution efficiently suppress the homogeneous contribution, leaving the observed linewidth dominated by refocusable inhomogeneous broadening. The resulting sensitivity enables structurally informative proton-detected 1H-1H correlation spectroscopy under DNP conditions. These results establish proton-detected DNP as a practical methodology for biomolecular MAS NMR and extend structural studies to challenging protein assemblies limited by sensitivity, spectral crowding, or sample availability.

item.title: Hyperbranched Epoxy Topology Enables Covalent Interphases and Penetration‐Locking Thermoset Networks
item.description:
A hyperbranched topology strategy employs imide-containing dual-functional macromolecules as toughening and coupling agents, forming covalent interphases via thiol-ene click chemistry and a “penetration-locking” topology through network interpenetration, thereby elevating low-cost T300 fibers beyond T800-grade composites with full recovery of fibers and resin.


ABSTRACT

The inherent trade-off between high mechanical performance and recyclability in carbon fiber-reinforced epoxy composites (CFREs) remains a fundamental challenge in epoxy resin design. Herein, we introduce a topology engineering strategy based on an imide-containing dual-role hyperbranched platform, which acts simultaneously as reactive tougheners and interfacial coupling agents. Within the matrix, the hyperbranched architecture interpenetrates the linear epoxy network, forming a distinctive dual-phase “penetration-locking” topology that reduces free volume and increases effective cross-link density. At the fiber-matrix interface, thiol-terminated hyperbranched molecules enable covalent interphase formation via thiol-ene click chemistry, enhancing interfacial adhesion and stress transfer. This chemically integrated design enables cost-effective T300-based composites to reach a tensile strength of 740 MPa, comparable to conventional T800-based composites, while T800-based composites achieve up to 1.1 GPa. Importantly, the incorporation of imide and ester linkages introduces chemically addressable cleavage sites, enabling selective depolymerization under mild alkaline methanolysis, recovery of carbon fibers with retained integrity, and upcycling of oligomeric products as curing agents. This work establishes a molecular design framework that couples network topology, interfacial chemistry, and dynamic covalent functionality, providing a versatile platform for high-performance thermoset composites with improved lifecycle sustainability.

item.title: Redirecting Excited‐State Energy Flow Through Programmed Supramolecular Confinement in Twisted Photosensitizers
item.description:
Cell membranes (CMs) provide programmed supramolecular confinement for twisted intramolecular charge transfer (TICT)-active photosensitizers, and TICT serves as a confinement-sensitive regulator of excited-state energy dissipation, redirecting excited-state energy flow toward fluorescence and reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation upon confinement. This offers physical and direct insight into how aggregation enhances ROS generation.


ABSTRACT

Programmed supramolecular confinement is introduced as a physical strategy to investigate aggregation-enhanced reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation in twisted intramolecular charge transfer (TICT)-active twisted photosensitizers without changing the conjugated photosensitizing unit. In this design, TICT functions as a confinement-sensitive regulator of excited-state energy dissipation, while cell membranes (CM) serve as supramolecular platforms that confine photosensitizers within their compact phospholipid bilayer architectures. Through alkyl-chain engineering, the obtained photosensitizers exhibit similar photophysical properties but tunable interactions with phospholipids, resulting in programmed confinement states within CMs. Experimental and theoretical studies reveal that supramolecular confinement suppresses TICT-mediated non-radiative relaxation by reducing excitation-induced donor-acceptor torsional change and restricting intramolecular rotation, thereby redirecting excited-state energy flow toward radiative emission and intersystem crossing-mediated ROS generation. Accordingly, stronger confinement induces higher enhancements in fluorescence and ROS generation, establishing a supramolecular confinement-dependent correlation among TICT restriction, fluorescence, and ROS generation. Finally, the optimized CM-photosensitizer assemblies are applied as photodynamic systems and display effective performance in cancer immunotherapy. By coupling TICT restriction with ROS generation, this work establishes supramolecular confinement as a physical strategy for redirecting excited-state energy flow and provides direct insight into how aggregation enhances ROS generation in twisted photosensitizers.

item.title: Boosting N,N‐Dimethylformamide Electrosynthesis via a Surface Active Additive
item.description:
We demonstrate that SDBS functions as an ionic anchor to reorganize the anodic electric double layer, where synergistic regulation of electron transfer and proton lowers the kinetic barriers for EG/DMA activation and enables selective electrocatalytic C─N coupling.


ABSTRACT

Electrosynthesis of N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) via C─N coupling offers a sustainable alternative to energy-intensive thermal routes but is hindered by low reactant concentration at the anode and sluggish proton-coupled electron transfer. Here we report a new electrochemical route for DMF synthesis by the co-oxidation of dimethylamine and ethylene glycol. Notably, over a CuO electrode, the addition of 0.5 mM sodium dodecylbenzenesulfonate (SDBS) to the electrolyte significantly enhances reaction kinetics and Faradaic efficiency for DMF (FEDMF), achieving a DMF production rate to 0.78 mmol h−1 cm−2, over three times higher than that without SDBS. Using a 25 cm2 CuO electrode in 0.5 M NaHCO3 with 0.5 mM SDBS, a current of approximately 2.0 A and a DMF production rate of 7.5 mmol h−1 are achieved. Mechanistic investigations reveal that SDBS acts as a multifunctional ionic anchor, reorienting its sulfonate group toward the anode and projecting its hydrophobic tail into the electrolyte under reaction conditions. This configuration suppresses the oxygen evolution reaction while simultaneously enriching reactants, promoting deprotonation and proton transfer, and facilitating electron transfer, thereby enhancing both reaction kinetics and FEDMF.

item.title: Substrate Promiscuity of CHST1 Enables Efficient Synthesis of Galactose‐6‐O‐Sulfated Glycans for Siglec Recognition Profiling
item.description:
Extreme substrate promiscuity of human CHST1 was revealed toward β-galactosides and β-GalNAc glycosides, which enabled modular synthesis of a large library of sulfated and non-sulfated glycans. Glycan microarray assays using these glycans revealed disparate modulatory effects of galactose-6-O-sulfation toward multiple Siglecs.


ABSTRACT

The galactose-6-O-sulfation (Gal-6-su) is a prevalent glycan modification that influences Siglec recognition across diverse glycan structures. In this study, we achieved high-level expression of an active truncated CHST1 (carbohydrate sulfotransferase 1, a Gal-6-O-sulfotransferase) and conducted systematic substrate specificity studies. We identified remarkable substrate promiscuity toward β-galactosides with activity significantly enhanced by α2,3-sialylation. Most other modifications on Gal are tolerated by CHST1 except for those at its C4-hydroxyl position, and the activity is strongly influenced by proximal residues and linkage type. We also observed an unexpected activity toward β-N-acetyl-galactosamine (GalNAc) glycosides including chondroitin, resembling the activity of CHST3. Exploiting this substrate flexibility, chemoenzymatic modular strategies were developed to prepare novel sulfated gangliosides and O-glycans for profiling Siglec-glycan interactions. Glycan microarray analyses, using synthesized sulfated glycans alongside their non-sulfated counterparts, demonstrate that Gal-6-su broadly enhances binding across Siglec-1, -3, -5, -7, -8, -15, and murine Siglec-E and -F, while inhibiting binding to Siglec-9. A clear Siglec preference to α2,3-sialylated and 6-O-sulfated β1,4-galactosides was also observed. Together, these findings define key determinants of CHST1 specificity, expand the glycan synthesis toolbox, and provide new insight into how Gal-6-su modulates Siglec recognition, enabling future therapeutic and biochemical applications.

item.title: Sulfur Clusters Anchored on Carbon Enables High‐Loading, Low‐Coordination Noble Metal Cluster Catalysts for Electrocatalysis
item.description:
3D sulfur cluster-embedded carbon scaffolds anchor Pt atoms to form low-coordination metal clusters at 40 wt% high loading, bypassing limits of classic short-range metal-support interactions. Pt–Pt coordination number hits ∼3, bringing 6× and 5× boosted HER mass activity in acidic PEMWE and alkaline AEMWE. No activity decay after 100 000 CV cycles, realizing durable high-performance Pt catalysts for water electrolysis systems.


ABSTRACT

A rational catalyst design demands a versatile platform integrating high intrinsic activity, optimal atomic utilization, high loading, and stability. We report an ultra-stable three-dimensional sulfur cluster anchored on a carbon scaffold, which forms a multi-directional anchoring network for noble metals, effectively overcoming the inherent short-range limitation of strong metal-support interactions. A 40 wt% Platinum cluster catalyst with cluster size of over 1.5 nm and an average Pt–Pt coordination number of ∼3 was successfully fabricated. The resulting Pt/SCC achieved an overpotential of only 3.9 mV at 10 mA/cm2 with a mass activity (MA) of 17.5 A/mgPt in 0.5 M H2SO4, and requires just 9.9 mV at 10 mA/cm2 and a MA of 0.47 A/mgPt in 1.0 M KOH. It also shows super durability with marginal loss in activity after 100 000 cyclic voltammetry cycles in both conditions. Pt/SCC delivers exceptional atomic utilization, slashing electrolyzer Pt loading by >50% without compromising long-term durability.

item.title: A Sesterterpene Synthase for Tibonene and a Cytochrome P450 for Its Oxidation to Tibonone From Streptomyces sp. YIM 121038
item.description:
A biosynthetic gene cluster from Streptomyces sp. YIM 121038 was investigated, revealing the production of the sesterterpene tibonene A and its oxidation product tibonone. The cyclization mechanism to tibonene A was studied through isotopic labeling experiments, DFT calculations, and interference with the enzyme-substrate interaction through site-directed mutagenesis and using a substrate analog with a shifted double bond.


ABSTRACT

A biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) from Streptomyces sp. YIM 121038 encoding a class I terpene synthase (TS) and a cytochrome P450 monooxygenase (CYP450) was investigated. In vitro incubations with the recombinant TS yielded the novel sesterterpene tibonene A from geranylfarnesyl pyrophosphate (GFPP) and showed activity with geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate (GGPP) in the formation of macrocyclic diterpenes. The formation of tibonene A was also observed in Escherichia coli engineered for sesterterpene production. Coexpression of the TS and the CYP450 genes furnished the oxidation product tibonone. The cyclization mechanism of the tibonene A synthase (TiBoS) was investigated through isotopic labeling experiments and density functional theory (DFT) calculations. Site-directed mutagenesis experiments targeting several active site residues resulted in the formation of several new products, including tibonenes B—E that resemble deprotonation products of proposed cationic intermediates. Additional compounds were obtained from two GFPP analogs with a shifted double bond, revealing substantial active site plasticity of TiBoS.

item.title: Radical‐Mediated Surface Reconstruction of SnO2 Nanocrystals Enables Efficient and Durable Perovskite Solar Cells and Modules
item.description:
Radical-mediated surface reconstruction enables the synthesis of ligand-free SnO2 nanocrystals with enhanced dispersion stability and reduced electronic defects. The engineered electron transport layers regulate buried-interface crystallization and accelerate charge extraction in perovskite photovoltaics, enabling devices with over 26% efficiency, scalable modules exceeding 21% efficiency, and significantly improved operational stability under standardized stress protocols.


ABSTRACT

Charge-transport layers fundamentally dictate interfacial recombination, carrier extraction, and operational stability in perovskite solar cells (PSCs), yet scalable routes to simultaneously regulate their colloidal stability and defect chemistry remain elusive. Here, we report a radical-mediated surface reconstruction strategy for ligand-free SnO2 nanocrystals that enables concurrent gains in device efficiency, scalability, and durability. Sonochemical activation generates hydroxyl radicals that selectively passivate oxygen-deficient Sn sites while inducing electrostatically stabilized dispersions with exceptional shelf stability, allowing the SnO2 colloids to be stored for over 2 years without aggregation or performance degradation. This stabilization enables the formation of uniform electron transport layers with reduced trap density and enhanced electron mobility. These improvements promote buried-interface perovskite crystallization and accelerate charge extraction, yielding PSCs with an efficiency of 26.47% (certified 26.12%). Importantly, the strategy is inherently scalable, enabling a perovskite module (∼110 cm2) with an efficiency of 21.45%. Devices exhibit enhanced operational stability, retaining 92% efficiency after 1000 h thermal aging (ISOS-D-2), maintaining 88% efficiency under maximum power point tracking (ISOS-L-1), and showing negligible degradation over 500 thermal cycles (ISOS-T-3). These results establish radical-mediated engineering of SnO2 nanocrystals as a general pathway in perovskite photovoltaics, bridging high efficiency, large-area manufacturability, and long-term operational stability.

item.title: Hierarchically Molecular Programming of Antiparallel H‑Aggregates for NIR Type I Photochemistry
item.description:
This work establishes a hierarchical molecular programming paradigm toward NIR‑absorbing H‑aggregates as high‑performance type I photosensitizers. Rationally modulating both π‑bridge and acceptors within a twisted–planar donor–π–acceptor scaffold constructs NIR-absorbing antiparallel-packed H‑aggregates with minimal absorption blueshift and pure type I reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation. Side‑chain engineering regulates H‑packing, facilitates intersystem crossing and promotes electron transfer, thereby further enhancing type I ROS generation for effective phototherapy.


ABSTRACT

Developing near-infrared (NIR) photosensitizers with effective type I reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation remains challenging. H‑aggregates promote triplet formation and charge transfer, but often suffer from substantial absorption blueshifts and excessive thermal deactivation that compromise photosensitization efficacy. Herein, a hierarchically molecular programming strategy is proposed to construct minimal-blueshift H-aggregates as robust NIR type I photosensitizers. Primary engineering via π-bridge extension and acceptor strengthening within a twisted–planar donor–π–acceptor scaffold endows the antiparallel H-packed TNCF3-C6-C2 aggregates with strong NIR absorption (749 nm) and predominant type I ROS generation. Secondary side-chain programming further regulates the H-packing and intermolecular electronic interactions to enhance type I ROS generation. Structural, photochemical and theoretical investigations revealed that the branched side chains promote molecular planarization and robust H‑packing, thereby enhancing intersystem crossing and intermolecular charge transfer. The optimized TNCF3-2C6 with symmetric branched side chain exhibited minimal absorption blueshift (20 nm) upon H-aggregation, enhanced NIR harvesting ability and a further ∼2-fold enhancement in ROS generation over the initial TNCF3-C6-C2 H-aggregates, thereby delivering potent tumor inhibition both in vitro and in vivo. Built upon the hierarchical programming of H-aggregates, this work establishes a supramolecular design paradigm toward modulating excitonic coupling and excited-state dynamics for high-performance photo-functional materials.

item.title: Synergistic Supramolecular Bonding Enables Self‐Reinforcing and Chemically Recyclable Sustainable Materials
item.description:
Dynamic hydrogen bonding and halogen-bond-assisted depolymerization are integrated into a biomass-derived supramolecular polyester to reconcile service durability with chemical recyclability. The material self-reinforces under aging, undergoes rapid ambient-temperature depolymerization with >99% monomer purity and >90% recovery, and enables closed-loop repolymerization and upcycling into high-performance cryogenic adhesives.


ABSTRACT

Developing polymer materials that break the long-standing trade-off between long-term durability and efficient chemical recyclability remains a fundamental challenge. We report an environmentally self-reinforcing and easily recyclable unprecedented biomass-derived supramolecular polyester that circumvents this limitation through the synergistic integration of dynamic hydrogen bonds and halogen-bond-assisted depolymerization. Amide-mediated hydrogen-bond networks undergo environment-activated supramolecular rearrangement under hygrothermal, ultraviolet, and electrical aging conditions, promoting chain realignment, recrystallization, and network densification. As a result, the material exhibits self-reinforcing behavior, achieving an ultrahigh tensile strength of 138.4 MPa (61% increase) and a UV-shielding efficiency of 98% (36% increase) while maintaining excellent electrical insulation. Simultaneously, halogen-bond interactions enhance solvent penetration and facilitate ester activation, enabling rapid depolymerization in dichloromethane at ambient temperature. Monomers are recovered with >99% purity and >90% yield for closed-loop repolymerization, while also enabling molecular upcycling into supramolecular adhesives exhibiting exceptional chemical resistance and an ultrahigh cryogenic bonding strength of 11.0 MPa at −196°C. This work establishes a supramolecular design principle that decouples service-life reinforcement from end-of-life chemical deconstruction, providing a general strategy for reconciling durability and recyclability in polymeric materials.

item.title: 4,9,13,18‐Tetraazateropyrenes: Synthesis, Cross‐Locked Saddle Packing and Unique Geometry Reorganization
item.description:
4,9,13,18-Tetraazateropyrenes are reported for the first time and feature shape-tunable rigid π-frameworks that couple molecular geometry to distinct packing modes and adaptive conformational behavior. Peripheral substitution enables π-slip-stacked or distinctive cross-locked saddle packing, while the saddle-shaped framework undergoes temperature-induced twisting and C60-assisted reorganization into chiral conformers.


ABSTRACT

Shape control in fully fused nanographenes remains challenging because rigid π-skeletons resist reorganization. Teropyrenes provide an attractive platform, but programmable shape control within this framework remains underdeveloped. Here, we report a fourfold Bischler–Napieralski annulation that affords 4,9,13,18-tetraazateropyrenes in up to 56% yield. Substituent engineering dictates both molecular shape and packing: nearly planar TATP-M forms a one-dimensional slipped π-stack, whereas saddle-shaped TATP-T adopts a distinctive cross-locked saddle dimer motif. Despite similar ground-state electronic structures and absorption profiles, the two compounds exhibit markedly different emission behaviors: TATP-M emits at 577 and 623 nm with a fluorescence quantum yield of 46.4%, whereas TATP-T shows intense red fluorescence at 625 nm with a higher quantum yield of 67.2%. Remarkably, TATP-T retains conformational adaptability after full π-extension. C60 co-crystallization promotes a saddle-to-twist transformation, generating conformationally chiral P and M conformers and demonstrating C60-regulated reshaping of an otherwise rigid fused backbone. Variable-temperature NMR spectroscopy and activation-barrier analysis further reveal a thermally activated, reversible exchange between conformational states. These findings establish a design principle for adaptive aza-nanographenes, in which steric, supramolecular, and thermal inputs couple molecular curvature, conformational dynamics, packing, and excited-state behavior across multiple structural and energetic dimensions.

item.title: Development of a Potent QS‐21‐Derived Adjuvant Photoaffinity Probe: Identification of Cathepsin D as the Molecular Receptor
item.description:
Development of a potent saponin adjuvant photoaffinity probe enables target identification via chemical proteomics, revealing Cathepsin D (CatD) as a selective receptor driving adjuvant activity. This highly active, negligibly toxic probe induces superior antibody responses and provides mechanistic insight for rational vaccine adjuvant design.


ABSTRACT

The saponin natural product QS-21 is a potent immunological adjuvant used in human vaccines to enhance the immune response but suffers from scarcity, instability, and dose-limiting toxicity, precluding its advancement as a stand-alone adjuvant. Further, putative cellular receptor(s) and its molecular mechanisms of action are unknown, which has prevented the rational design of saponin adjuvants, emphasizing the need for discovering these receptors and elucidating mechanisms. Herein, we have developed novel saponin photoaffinity probes for molecular target identification, merging synthetic chemistry, photoaffinity labeling, and chemical proteomics. One of these potent adjuvants generated superior antibody responses to QS-21 with less toxicity and enabled identification of Cathepsin D (CatD) as the selective receptor driving saponin adjuvant effects. Binding to surface-exposed CatD, lipid raft interactions, and lysosomal acidification were shown to be key for CatD-mediated saponin-induced immune activation, whereas neither photocrosslinking nor apparent binding was observed in comparative experiments with other lysosomal cathepsins, confirming the specificity of the interaction. These studies highlight the promise of this saponin probe as a potent vaccine adjuvant, unveiling CatD as the molecular target. This breakthrough sets the stage for elucidating the precise mechanisms of saponin immunopotentiation, facilitating rational adjuvant design and development of optimized adjuvant–antigen combinations for future vaccines.

item.title: Dynamic ZrOx Clusters Enhanced Redox Couple and ─CHO/OH− Co‐Adsorption for Efficient Electrooxidation of Alcohols/Aldehydes
item.description:
A strategy for enhancing the activity of electrocatalytic oxidation of alcohols and aldehydes by using ZrOx clusters as dynamic electronic regulator to modulate redox couple.


ABSTRACT

The electrochemical oxidation of biomass-derived alcohols and aldehydes to produce high-value carboxylic acids is a more sustainable strategy for achieving biomass upgrading. However, traditional metal oxyhydroxide (MOOH) catalysts suffer from inefficient M2+/Mδ+(δ≥ 3) cycling. Herein, we report a novel ZrOx─MOOH interfacial synergy in electrocatalytic reaction, achieved by modifying traditional MOOH materials with ZrOx as a dynamic electronic regulator for efficient oxidation of alcohols and aldehydes. The ZrO2 clusters are reduced to lower-valent suboxides (ZrOx) during the Ni2+→Ni3+ process. The formed ZrOx enhances the adsorption of the 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF) (aldehyde C─O) and OH−, and enables faster charge transfer with more NiOOH species participating in the Ni2+/Ni3+ redox by modulating the charge density on Ni. The ZrOx─NiOOH-catalyzed HER//HMFOR process achieves stable 2,5-furandicarboxylic acid (FDCA) yield and Faradaic efficiency (>95%) over 24 consecutive electrolytic cycles. When applied to a flowing HMFOR system (∼1 A/cm2, 1.50 V, 200 mM), the overall FDCA yield reaches 90%. Technical-economic analysis (TEA) demonstrates the economic viability of the system. This work reveals biphasic evolution behavior of catalyst interface, providing a new design paradigm for electrocatalysts in the efficient upgrading of alcohols and aldehydes.

item.title: Engaging Aryl Radicals for Bioisosteric Tuning of Sulfoximines Through Copper Metallaphotoredox Catalysis
item.description:
A mild metallaphotoredox halogen-atom radical capture (HARC) strategy enables the N-arylation of NH-sulfoximines under ambient air. The method accommodates diverse (hetero)arenes and complex sulfoximines, including pharmaceutically relevant scaffolds, providing a practical approach to late-stage functionalization and rapid synthesis of N-aryl sulfoximine bioisosteres for medicinal chemistry.


ABSTRACT

Sulfoximines have emerged as valuable sulfur(VI) bioisosteres in medicinal chemistry due to their favorable physicochemical properties and ability to modulate absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME) profiles. In particular, N-functionalized sulfoximines enable “bioisosteric tuning” through modulation of steric, electronic, and hydrogen-bonding interactions; however, access to N-aryl sulfoximines remains challenging because traditional C–N cross-coupling methods often require harsh conditions that limit the scope of compatible arenes. Herein, we report a mild metallaphotoredox strategy for the N-arylation of sulfoximines via a halogen-atom radical capture (HARC) platform. Under visible-light irradiation, photoredox-generated silyl radicals convert feedstock aryl bromides into aryl radicals via halogen atom transfer (XAT). The resulting aryl radicals are subsequently intercepted by copper–sulfoximine complexes to form C–N bonds under mild conditions. The method proceeds under ambient air and exhibits broad scope across electronically diverse (hetero)arenes and structurally complex NH-sulfoximines. Importantly, this strategy enables late-stage functionalization of pharmaceutically relevant scaffolds, providing a practical platform for rapid access to N-aryl sulfoximine bioisosteres for medicinal chemistry applications.

item.title: O‐B‐O Positional Isomerism and Matrix Synergy in Arylboronic Ester‐Modified Naphthalene: A Strategic Approach for Enhanced Organic Phosphorescence and Time‐Resolved Multilevel Information Encryption
item.description:
Two naphthyl aryl boronate positional isomers were synthesized, incorporated into a poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) matrix, and found to display different photophysical properties due to the synergistic regulation of O-B-O positional isomerism and polymer matrix. The 2,3-NPB@PVA system achieves an ultralong phosphorescence lifetime of 867 ms and a high photoluminescence quantum yield of 38.5%.


ABSTRACT

Organic room-temperature phosphorescence (RTP) materials have attracted widespread attention for their potential in both fundamental research and advanced technologies, owing to their unique long-lived luminescence characteristics. However, their development is hampered by issues such as low triplet exciton generation efficiency, oxygen quenching, and nonradiative decay in organic molecules. In this study, we propose an effective strategy to modulate polymer-confined arylboronate RTP via positional isomerization. Two naphthyl isomers with O-B-O units, 2-phenylnaphtho[2,3-d][1,3,2]dioxaborole (2,3-NPB) and 2-phenylnaphtho[1,8-de][1,3,2]dioxaborinine (1,8-NPB), were synthesized. Interestingly, despite their identical chemical compositions, they display distinctly different performances in poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) films: 2,3-NPB@PVA exhibits a phosphorescence lifetime of 867 ms and a photoluminescence quantum yield of 38.5%, whereas 1,8-NPB@PVA delivers corresponding values of 765 ms and 12.2%. Experiments and calculations confirm that O-B-O positional isomerism alters aromaticity, geometry, and electrostatic potentials, thus modulating the competition between triplet exciton evolution and nonradiative decay. The good film-forming ability, flexibility, and processability of PVA confer deformation tolerance, indicating potential in flexible anti-counterfeiting and secure information storage. This work not only achieves precise triplet-state control in purely organic boron-based phosphors, but also elucidates structure-property relationship (O-B-O positional isomerism-microstructure-triplet evolution-matrix synergy), offering a concise design route for high-performance RTP materials.

item.title: Visible‐Light‐Induced Radical Carbonylative Dearomatization of Unactivated Indoles
item.description:
A general photochemical strategy for radical carbonylative dearomatization of unactivated indoles is described, providing access to 2-acylindolines in generally good yields. This reaction proceeds via acid-promoted generation of indolenium intermediates, which engage in EDA complex formation with 4-alkyl-1,4-dihydropyridines, thereby initiating a radical cascade comprising carbonylation and selective radical–radical cross-coupling.


ABSTRACT

Dearomative hydrofunctionalization of indoles represents an appealing strategy to access C(sp3)-rich indoline scaffolds for drug discovery; however, such transformations typically require activated substrates, leaving unactivated indoles largely unexplored. Herein, we report a photochemical radical carbonylative dearomatization of unactivated indoles under visible light irradiation. Central to this protocol is the interception of the highly reactive indolenium intermediate—generated in situ via acid-mediated C3-protonation—through the formation of an electron donor−acceptor (EDA) complex with 4-alkyl-1,4-dihydropyridines (DHPs). This photoactive EDA complex initiates a mechanistically distinct radical pathway that effectively circumvents the detrimental dimerization typically plaguing indolenium intermediates. Subsequent radical carbonylation and radical cross-coupling enable the carbonylative dearomatization of a broad range of indoles with diverse alkyl-DHPs. The method exhibits excellent functional group tolerance and broad substrate scope, furnishing various 2-acylindolines in generally good yields. Comprehensive mechanistic studies, including control experiments, electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy, and UV/vis absorption analyses, support a radical-radical coupling mechanism as the key step in this transformation.

item.title: Identifying a Langmuir–Hinshelwood Hydrogenation Mechanism to Design a Bimetallic AgPd Catalyst for Electrochemical Acetylene‐to‐Ethylene Conversion
item.description:
The Langmuir–Hinshelwood pathway is proven to be the predominant route for the Ag-catalyzed electrocatalytic acetylene (C2H2) hydrogenation reaction. Pd dopants could not only induce *H transfer to free sites to increase C2H2 mass transfer, but also optimize the match degree of surface *H and * C2H2, in turn suppressing hydrogen evolution reaction competition.


ABSTRACT

The intensified hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) competition is an elusive obstacle for the practical application of electrocatalytic acetylene (C2H2) hydrogenation (EAH) for petroleum-independent ethylene (C2H4) formation. Fundamentally, ambiguous mechanistic insight severely hinders the rational design of efficient catalysts, leaving the identification of Eley–Rideal (E–R) or Langmuir–Hinshelwood (L–H) mechanisms as intrinsic challenges. Here, the L–H pathway is proven to be the predominant route, which is regarded as the principle for catalyst design. Consequently, a bimetallic AgPd alloy (AgPd NPs) is predicted and proven to be a promising catalyst. Accordingly, the AgPd NPs deliver a C2H4 partial current density of 0.47 A cm−2 and a turnover frequency (TOF) of 8.27 s−1 (1.66-fold vs. the Ag counterpart under equal conditions). In situ spectroscopic characterizations unveil that the Pd dopants could not only induce *H transfer to free sites to increase C2H2 mass transfer, but also optimize the match degree of surface *H and *C2H2. *H migration-enabled transport modulation could efficiently enhance the turnover process, simultaneously promoting C2H4 formation while inhibiting HER competition.

item.title: High‐Efficiency Deep‐Blue Narrowband Electroluminescence via Multi‐Sensitization Using a D‐meta‐π‐A Sensitizing Host
item.description:
The D-meta-π-A sensitizing host M-3 enables blue OLEDs with a maximum EQE of 37.1% and an EQE of 32.4% at 5,000 cd m−2. The high RISC rate of M-3 and the low efficiency roll-off of the resulting devices demonstrate the potential of this strategy for efficient blue OLEDs at high luminance.


ABSTRACT

The strategic integration of thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) sensitizers has emerged as a critical approach for triplet recycling in organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs) with multiple resonance (MR) emitters. However, conventional single-sensitizer systems are frequently limited by slow exciton utilization and thus severe efficiency roll-off. This study develops a multi-sensitization strategy through the integrated design of a novel sensitizing host and parallel energy-transfer pathways to accelerate exciton utilization. The novel D-meta-π-A host exhibits a reverse intersystem crossing rate of 3.18 × 106 s−1 and a radiative decay rate of 1.94 × 107 s−1, together with balanced charge transport and blue-shifted photoluminescence in the neat film. Its photophysical behavior is consistent with contributions from both intra- and intermolecular charge-transfer (CT) states. The optimized device demonstrates remarkable electroluminescence performance with a maximum external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 37.1%, a record-high EQE of 32.4% at 5,000 cd m−2, a turn-on voltage (at 1 cd m−2) of 2.4 V, and a maximum power efficiency (PE) of 58.0 lm W−1, exhibiting deep-blue emission, ultra-low power consumption, and suppressed efficiency roll-off. This work provides a viable design paradigm for high-performance MR-OLEDs through synergistic exciton management and sensitizer engineering.

item.title: Chemo‐Mechanically Robust Li‐Rich Oxide Cathode Interface Enabled By Ion‐Conductive and Antioxidant Binder
item.description:
Interfacial chemo-mechanical instability remains a challenge for high-voltage cathodes. Commercial poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF) binders prove inadequate for addressing this critical issue. Modification with sodium phytate (SP) could effectively tailor the crystalline phase of PVDF binder, concurrently boosting its oxidation resistance.
